full_judgment:
2. Respondents' predecessor instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 130 of 1973 in the 2nd court of Munsif, Comilla against the appellant for pre-emption. The case was allowed exparte on August 30, 1974 granting pre-emption against her. Appellant filed an application under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, being Miscellaneous Case No. 39 of 1978, for setting aside the exparte order. Grounds stated in the application were that the notice of the preemption case was fraudulently suppressed and she had no knowledge of the institution of the case against her till February 23, 1978. In an application for bail by the accused in G.R. Case No. 512 of 1977 which was started at her instance the fact regarding the pre-emption case was disclosed. The notice of the pre-emption case was sent to the address of her husband's paternal home in village Doshpara, P.S. Daudkandi, whereas she, being a school Teacher at Narayangonj, had been living in Dhaka at the relevant time. 

 4. Application for restoration of the pre-emption case was rejected by the Munsif on June 18, 1979. Against this order the appellant filed Civil Revision No.32 of 1979 in the court of District Judge, Commilla stating that the notice was not issued at the proper address where the appellant was living and was shown to have been served by hanging in dwelling hut at village Doshpara. Further, due to non service of the notice or for not serving it according to the provisions of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure she was not aware of the pre-emption case and therefore, could not challenge the exparte order within the period of limitation. The case was dismissed by the District Judge. The appellant moved the High Court Division against the order of dismissal but with no success. 

 5. Being aggrieved, appellant moved this Court and obtained leave to appeal on the contentions that the High Court Division, without considering the question whether in serving the summons the provisions of Rule 9, 15 and 17 of Order 5, C.P.C. and also those of Civil Rules and Order were complied with as it was a case of service by hanging, proceeded merely on the evidence of the process server to reach the conclusion that the service was a good service. Further, the High Court Division was wrong in totally omitting to consider the appellant's evidence. 

 6. It appears that the process server who deposed regarding the service of notice by him at her village home at Doshpara stated that the appellant was not present when he served it by hanging. This may not contradict the process server's earlier statement that he tendered the notice to the appellant who refused to accept the same whereupon he affixed it on the outer door of her house, but is sufficient to raise doubts as to the service of the notice by hanging, particularly in view of the appellant's strong denial. The learned Judge of the High Court Division did not consider the evidence of the appellant to the effect and that she used to live at Dhaka permanently and was not at her village home at the relevant time. Moreover, she being a school Teacher attended the school at Narayangonj on the relevant date. Apart from this the first appellate court found on evidence that the appellant actually resided at Dhaka at the relevant time. If so, and. in view of the finding that she being Assistant Head Mistress in a Girls' School at Narayangonj permanently lives in Dhaka, it is not understood why her address in the pre-emption case was shown at village Doshpara. Appellant did not dispute that her husband who died in 1964 left properties there which she used to look after. In order to establish that notice could have been served at either of the addresses, that is, at Dhaka where she lives permanently and at Doshpara where she occasionally resides, reference was made to Explanation I to section 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This provides that a person who has a permanent dwelling house at one place and has a temporary residence at another place shall be deemed to reside at both places. So, if notice is served at either of these places, no illegality attaches to it. The point for enquiry is not as to whether the notice could have been served at the appellant's temporary residence at Doshpara instead of at Dhaka where she claims to reside permanently, but the enquiry should have been directed as to whether the notice in question has been served in accordance with law, and in view of the challenge to the service of notice whether there has been proper verification as laid down in Rules 17 and 19 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. As the challenge to the service of notice at Doshpara is not merely verbal but sought to be substantiated with reference to a certificate granted by the Head Mistress of the School where the appellant was Assistant Head Mistress that she did not take any leave in August 1974 and further, her evidence as to her permanently residing in Dhaka, it was necessary to conform to the provisions of law regarding the service of notice. In support of his contention that the service return has not been verified in accordance with the provisions of Rules 17, 19 and 19A of Order 5, C.P.C. and Rule 92(2) (iv)of Civil Rules and Orders, Vol. 1. Mr. Ahmed, Counsel for the appellant, referred to the case of Mst. Johara begum V. Rafiqul Kader. (1973) 25 DLR 91. Since we find from the evidence of the process server that neither the appellant nor her son was present at the time of service of notice and also that the appellant evidence was not at all considered by the Court below, the notice of the pre-emption case cannot be accepted as having been duly served upon her. 

 7. The appeal is allowed. Judgments and Order of the Courts below are set aside and the exparte order dated 30-8-74 is set aside. We, however' pass no order for restoration of the land in question. There will be no order as to costs. The original case must be heard expeditiously.
